                           G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’
                 REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        G-9 and G-13 Landowners1 files this Reply to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision

(PFD) for consideration by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) and respectfully

shows as follows:

                                      I.         INTRODUCTION

        Since the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) was approved, circumstances have

changed and serious concerns have been raised regarding the factual underpinnings of the Electric

Reliability Council of Texas’ (ERCOT) PBRP and whether the ongoing 765-kV transmission line

projects are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public (i.e.

“need”). The concerns regarding the need for these projects, including Import Path 2 (Bell County

East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to- Sand Lake) are not limited to the parties in the proceedings before




        1
           The G-9 and G-13 Landowners include Jeff Kubin acting in the interest of The Highgate West Group LLC

(owners of tracts 2127 and 2128), and James Giddens acting in the interest of JKME Family Limited Partnership
(owners of tracts 2147 and 5142).

                                                       2
 the Commission. The same lawmakers who approved House Bill 5066 directing ERCOT to

develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin are now expressing serious reservations with the

plan and the 765-kV import paths themselves. In this docket alone, the following documents have

been filed by lawmakers underscoring their concerns and the need for a denial or delay:

                  •   Ex Parte Letter (including a letter from Texas State Senator
                      Donna Campbell to the Commissioners) filed on September

         In addition to these filings, Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick made a public statement on a

social media platform, X, calling for denial of the 765-kV applications.2 Lieutenant Governor

Patrick’s call for denial stems from the July 2026 Senate Business and Commerce Committee

hearing which lasted 15 hours at which legislators and hundreds of landowners expressed concerns

with the 765-kV transmission lines.3 A similar public statement calling for denial of the 765-kV

applications was made by Senator Charles Schwertner after the same July 2026 Senate Business

and Commerce Committee hearing.4 Both Lieutenant Governor Patrick and Senator Schwertner

note concerns over the need for these projects, landowners’ issues with the certificate of

convenience and necessity process, lack of proper notice from utilities, and the expedited nature

of the proceedings which lead to their calls for denial of the 765-kV applications. The Texas

House of Representatives Committee on State Affairs held a similar hearing on August 19, 2026

and equally strong and serious concerns were again raised by legislators, landowners, and

interested parties.

        Similar to these lawmakers’ filings in the docket and their public statements, the

Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) correctly determined that (1) the changed circumstances

leading to a change in projected load since the PBRP do not support the proposed Import Path 2

projects and (2) Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service

Corporation (collectively, Applicants) failed to show that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service

to the ALJs’ conclusions based on the Commission's decision in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315

(making up Import Path 1) and the weight that ERCOT’s recommendation should carry. 6 As

discussed in depth below, the individual Import Path projects should be evaluated independently,

and the change in circumstances resulting in a decrease in ERCOT’s forecasted load undermines

the weight that ERCOT’s PBRP guidance should carry. For these reasons, in addition to the ALJs’

analysis, the PFD is correct in concluding the need was not satisfied. Accordingly, the G-9 and

G-13 Landowners respectfully request the Commission approve the ALJs’ recommendation to

deny the Import Path 2 projects.

        In the event the Commission does not deny the Import Path 2 projects, the G-9 and G-13

Landowners disagree with the ALJs’ alternative recommendation that Route 894 be selected.7 As

discussed in the G-9 and G-13 Landowners’ Exceptions, the ALJs’ routing recommendation and

392, 487, and 894, the ALJs would have seen that Route 296 outperforms those routes. 10 The G-

9 and G-13 Landowners maintain their position that Route 296 should be selected because it out

performs the other Focus Routes and alternative routes. For the reasons discussed in Exceptions

and this Reply, in the event the Commission does not deny the Import Path 2 projects, the G-9 and

                            II.      PRELIMINARY ORDER (ISSUES 1-4)

A. Application Adequacy (Issue 1)

        The G-9 and G-13 Landowners do not address the Application adequacy issues.

B. Notice (Issues 2-3)

        Applicants and Commission Staff except to the PFD’s finding that the Applicants did not

meet the public meeting requirement under 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 22.52(a)(4).11

Applicants and Commission Staff both relied upon Commission precedent in making this

argument.12 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) (Rule 22.52) states that “[t]he utility must hold at least one

public meeting prior to the filing of its licensing application if 25 or more persons would be entitled

to receive direct mail notice of the application.”13 As the PFD correctly concludes, despite the

Applicants holding “at least one public meeting” before filing its application, the Applicants did

not meet the 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) standard since the “at least one” public meeting requirement is

a minimum tied to the number of persons entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application.14

        Here, the modifications made by Applicants after the three public meetings resulted in

Applicants’ expanding the study area and adding 400 miles of new route links impacting 1,400

additional landowners who were entitled to receive direct mail notice of the Application.15 The

1,400 landowners far exceed the “25 persons” standard in Rule 22.52. By not holding an additional

Applicants did not hold an additional public meeting after adding new route links that impact 1,400

new landowners, the ALJs were correct in finding the Applicants did not comply with Rule 22.52.

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners do not address Public Input issues.

                  III.     ISSUE RAISED BY THE PARTIES: DUE PROCESS

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners appreciate and agree with the ALJs’ summary of the

various due process issues and concerns raised due to the compressed procedural schedule and

notice problems.17

                                       IV.     NEED (ISSUES 5-7)

       The Applicants continue to rely almost exclusively on the PBRP as proof of “need” for the

Import Path 2 transmission line projects in the current docket and in Docket No. 59182.18

However, circumstances since the approval of the PBRP have changed which has resulted in the

same lawmakers who approved House Bill 5066 to now question the need for all projects included

in the PBRP and ERCOT’s projected load analysis.19 In addition to these lawmakers, the Texas

Public Policy Foundation (TPPF) expressed its concerns with the 765-kV projects back in

 December 19, 2025.20 The American Stewards of Liberty requested abatement of the proceeding

due to its concerns with the magnitude of the 765-kV projects and in order to allow the legislature

to address the issue.21 The TPPF filed a substantive letter in support of that motion.22

        The Applicants’ exceptions assert that the PFD disregarded the legislative intent that the

PBRP be completed expeditiously.23 However, many of the legislators responsible for the PBRP

have now made it clear that there should be a delay in these 765-kV transmission projects. Further,

the passage of House Bill 5066 was to direct ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the Permian

Basin, not to direct ERCOT to design and authorize the construction of a statewide 765-kV

transmission backbone.24 This intent is seen in the documents filed by lawmakers in this

proceeding and undermines the “great weight” Applicants assert should be given to ERCOT’s

PBRP in supporting Import Path 2.

        Applicants assert that under Commission Rules, “great weight” is to be given to ERCOT.25

However, PURA requires the Commission to “consider the historical load, forecasted load growth,

and additional load currently seeking interconnection.…”26 This is exactly what the ALJs did in

recommending Import Path 2 projects be denied because the need for the reliability transmission

project was not met. The ALJs not only took the PBRP into consideration, they also considered

the projected non-oil and gas load which was adjusted by ERCOT and reduced the forecasted non-

 oil and gas load by at least 3,571 MW. The ALJs also took into consideration the PBRP’s projected

oil and gas demand which came from one study, the 2022 S&P Global Study, which was found by

the ALJs to be unsubstantiated by ERCOT, flawed, overstated, and outdated.27 The PFD notes

that the S&P Global Study projected 10.3 GW of oil and gas load by 2030 compared to ERCOT’s

long-term forecasted 3.1 GW of oil and gas load.28 Although the ALJs did take the PBRP into

consideration and gave weight to the plan, they also took ERCOT’s forecasted load growth into

consideration. Therefore, the ALJs properly acted within PURA and Commission Rules and their

findings and conclusions are well grounded.

       Applicants further assert that the 39 GW of conventional generation capacity in the

Permian Basin region relied upon in the PFD is made up of “merely hypotheticals that do not

establish committed, deliverable capacity.”29                Applicants note that “not a single generator

presented evidence of its intention to build new generation capacity in West Texas.”30 While this

is not entirely incorrect, the same argument could be made for the speculative nature of the

forecasted load growth in the Permian Basin. The PFD notes that “the PBRP non-oil and gas load

forecast developed by ERCOT was a based on information given to it by transmission service

providers, including officer attestation letters, which included demand yet to sign an

interconnection agreement.”31 Since the PBRP was approved, the forecasted load has changed and

remains a prediction of future load. Thus, this forecast is not a concrete number and, instead, is

an estimate similar to the 39 GW of conventional generation capacity relied upon in the PFD.

          Applicants argue that no other party challenging the need for Import Path 2 projects

conducted independent studies or analysis that would rebut ERCOT’s work.32 This argument,

however, places an unjustified burden on intervenors and should be disregarded.                              Several

intervenors highlighted uncertainty in the need for the Import Path 2 projects and ongoing reports

and studies initiated by ERCOT. For example, the PFD discusses the 2022 ERCOT West Texas

Load Study by the University of Texas Bureau of Economic Geology and The Economic

Assessment of the 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan report by TPPF noting that

ERCOT’s most recent long term load forecast further shows that the S&P Global forecast which

was relied upon in the PBRP was overwrought.33 Intervenors also highlighted the Good Cause

Exception Request filed in May 2025 by ERCOT to reduce the loads for submitted officer-letter-

attestations and data centers.34 Additionally, intervenors highlighted the recent June 18, 2026

Commission Order requiring ERCOT to rework its large load forecasts using the newly adopted

Batch Zero process.35 Thus, it is reasonable for the ALJs to rely upon the shortcomings of the

PBRP and ongoing changes to ERCOT’s forecasted load.

         Applicants rely on the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) to show that

ERCOT continues to recommend the three 765-kV import paths as projects needed by 2030 to

maintain transmission reliability statewide.36 However, the 2025 RTP also recognizes that the

 challenges resulting from unprecedented load growth result in the need for continued review of

planning practices and policies.37 Specifically, the 2025 RTP states,

                  Unprecedented load growth, insufficient generation to meet this
                  demand, and the faster pace of load interconnections compared to
                  transmission and generation development moved the ERCOT
                  Region into a new era of planning. These challenges are further
                  compounded by ongoing changes in the resource mix. The locations
                  of both load and generation are crucial in driving flow patterns and
                  determining transmission needs. While the generation
                  interconnection queue offers some insight into future generation
                  development, the location of loads is less predictable, especially
                  given the much shorter lead times for load interconnections. This
                  adds complexity to transmission planning, as flow patterns and
                  stressed import paths may change between planning cycles.
                  Planning practices and policies must be reviewed to address these
                  new challenges. ERCOT has been and will continue to work with
                  stakeholders to identify the necessary changes in the planning
                  processes to ensure system reliability.38

        Even ERCOT acknowledges that this process is a continuing and ever-changing process.

Lawmakers are now calling for a further reevaluation of this process based on changed

circumstances since the Commission’s approval of the PBRP. Therefore, it is reasonable to deny

or delay Import Path 2 to allow for a proper evaluation of the need and if there may be any

necessary changes to ensure system reliability.

        Finally, Applicants and Commission Staff rely on the Commission’s approval of Import

Path 1, where it was found Oncor met its burden regarding need.39 However, Import Path 1 and

Import Path 2 are separate import paths and should be considered independently. Specifically,

looking at Import Path 2, the ALJs correctly determined that there are concerns regarding the

 availability of generation to provide power to the Permian Basin.40 The 2025 RTP emphasizes

that Central Texas faces the challenge of needing additional import capability. 41 The PFD

correctly notes that Applicants failed to show that Import Path 2 has specific generation resources

to import power to the Permian Basin.42 Further, as the record shows, there has been a decrease

in proposed megawatts needed in the Permian Basin. Thus, it is important to look at each proposed

import path that was recommended in the PBRP and determine whether each import path is still

needed based on the changing circumstances.

         As established earlier, the issue of need for the Import Path 2 projects is not a concern

limited to the intervening landowners in this proceeding. It is a legitimate concern felt by the

lawmakers who adopted House Bill 5066 calling for the creation of the PBRP. As a consequence

of the changing circumstances and adjusted forecasted load discussed in this Reply to Exceptions,

the Proposal for Decision, and the facts developed throughout this proceeding, the Commission

should adopt the ALJs’ recommendation and deny Import Path 2 due to a failure of Applicants to

show that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of

the public.

                            V.          ROUTING CRITERIA (ISSUES 8-10)

proximity of Links F6 and F34 (located on Route 296) to Florence Elementary School.43

        For instance, John Griffin Yates Jr. urges the Commission to approve Route 392,

contending that this concern related to Route 296 is answered by Route 392.46 The Solana

Intervenors and Brady Creek Intervenors similarly support the selection of Route 392.47

Route 392, however, performs poorly compared to Route 296 when reviewing the totality of

routing criteria. Route 392 is more impactful to the community as the proposed route crosses

within 520 feet from 136 habitable structures (31 more than Route 296).48 Route 392 is the most

expensive of the Focus Routes, the longest of the Focus Routes, runs about 5 miles further across

riparian areas than Route 296, and has 29 more recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet of

the centerline.49 Based on a review of all of the statutory criteria, Route 296 is a superior route

compared to Route 392.
